1.point: Two chains of names, Shia and Sufi, both start at the Prophet and then Ali; the chapter will show the shared road and source and why its authority belongs to the Imam alone.
steps: The Shia reader already recites a chain of names (Dua Tawassul)
A Sufi disciple receives a chain of names too, and it also begins Prophet then Ali
So the difference must lie further along the chain; state the chapter's claim

2.point: A Sufi order is a path that, long after the first seekers, hardened into an institution defined by its chain, its method and the obedience it demands.
steps: Define tariqa and its three features: chain, method, demands on the disciple
Show that orders arose centuries after the early seekers
Show what the institution added (system, rites, total obedience)
Set up the chain question for the next section

3.point: Nearly every order's chain ends at Imam Ali, so Sufi and Shia seekers have one source.
steps: State that the chains lead to Ali (Tabatabai's count of orders)
Show the rule holds even for a founder far from Shiism (Suhrawardi)
Note the one exception that justifies 'almost'
Observe that the chain idea itself is a Shia idea of inheritance
Conclude one source and hand on to the path question

4.point: Shia and Sufis walk the same path, but since no one technique suits every soul, the traveller needs an experienced guide rather than an order's technique.
steps: Shia share the orders' path, remembrance and books
What distinguishes orders is technique; show two techniques far apart
Both work, so there is no single method
Reason: each soul is its own channel and grace takes the soul's own shape
Paths are many but bounded within Islam and its law
Hence the traveller needs someone who has walked the road to read his own case

5.point: Shia masters borrowed teacher, robe and pledge from the orders but never gave them the authority that belongs to the Imams.
steps: Obedience to a chain of masters is what Shia do not share, because the Prophet's inner knowledge passed to the Imams
Shia masters came to stand outside the orders
Yet they used the orders' forms: contract, robe, pledge
Amuli himself says those forms carried no authority; what came, came from God
What accompanies the traveller throughout is the Imam; the teacher is left behind
So the forms sit under the Imam and the chain a Shia holds to is the Imams'

¶1.label: advance

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Second half of the comparison: the Sufi licence's chain, also starting Prophet then Ali.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Draws the comparison into the question and states what the chapter will establish, with the earlier-ground recall kept to one sentence.

¶4.label: advance

¶5.label: advance

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Supplies the 'became an institution' step: Tabatabai's description of the vast independent system the orders added.

¶7.label: support
¶7.why: Illustrates total obedience (the ghusl image); Section 5 ¶31 picks up obedience as the feature Shia do not share and this paragraph announces that hand-off.

¶8.label: support
¶8.why: Shows the chain branched and was contested; ¶31 relies on it explicitly ('As the first section showed, the orders' chains branched').

¶9.label: restate
¶9.why: Summarises the three features already given in ¶4 and ¶6; only the final transition sentence is new.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: States the section's claim with Tabatabai's count: all branches culminate in Ali.

¶11.label: support
¶11.why: The hard case (Suhrawardi, who claimed descent from Abu Bakr, yet whose own licence reaches Ali) that makes 'almost without exception' credible.

¶12.label: aside

¶13.label: support
¶13.why: Names the one exception, which the 'almost' in ¶10 and in the point needs.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Turns the genealogical fact into a doctrinal one: the chain idea itself is a Shia idea of an heir to the Prophet's inner knowledge, which ¶16 and Section 5 use.

¶15.label: aside
¶15.why: A second scholar going further (the qutb matches the Imam); the point of one source is reached without it and nothing after ¶16 uses the pole.

¶16.label: restate
¶16.why: Concludes what ¶10, ¶11 and ¶14 already established and hands on to the next section.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Supplies the 'path is shared' step with the shared remembrance.

¶18.label: support
¶18.why: Evidence for the shared books, which ¶17's opening sentence claims and ¶30 repeats.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Supplies the step that orders differ by technique and gives the first of the two contrasting techniques.

¶20.label: support
¶20.why: The second technique, needed for ¶21's 'both techniques have worked'.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Draws the conclusion that there is no single method, with the Sheikh's reasoning.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Gives the reason: each soul is its own channel; no two experiences repeat.

¶27.label: advance
¶27.why: Adds the hadith of many paths and the limit that the paths are many within Islam, which ¶28 and ¶30 build on.

¶28.label: advance

¶29.label: advance

¶30.label: restate

¶33.label: advance

¶34.label: support

¶35.label: advance

¶36.label: advance
